name: Carla Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Carla, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign for anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. This is a made-up study built around people like you, and there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week starts with algorithms on Monday morning and a linear algebra tutorial I'm slightly afraid of. I use an AI assistant every day, mostly to explain proofs I don't follow and to quiz me before tutorials. Tuesday evenings I run a small study group of eight people in a seminar room, and on Sundays I tutor two school kids in maths online for pocket money. I live in a shared flat with a medical student who studies at 3 a.m., so I wear earplugs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you choose computer science?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mum lectures in sociology and my dad works for the city council, so I grew up with dinner-table arguments about how systems treat people. I got into code at fourteen by making a little app that sorted our recycling days. I had top grades, my parents pay the fees and rent, and I have no debt, so I can afford to experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool that was oversold, and that's fine. I'd tell friends to keep learning the basics anyway, because if the tools stall, people who understand how things work are the ones who are still valuable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel a bit disappointed, to be honest. I find this stuff exciting and I'd like it to be as big as people say. But I'd also feel relieved for my parents, whose jobs stay as they are, and I'd be fine either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, keep using the assistant to learn faster, and put more hours into my study group. I'd apply for a summer job at a software company, probably a small one where you do a bit of everything. I'd also keep tutoring, since I enjoy it and it's money I earn myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm, if slightly flat. Like a festival where the headline act cancels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound almost wistful about it. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I think there's a lot of good that could come from it, like better medical tools and teaching help for kids who don't get much. If it's mostly hype, those things come slower. I'd miss that more than I'd miss any job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's now doubting their course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friend to stay, because a degree still teaches you how to think, and that doesn't expire. I'd show them how I use the assistant as a coach, not a copy machine, and then ask what they actually enjoy.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** that was oversold, and fine as that.
I'd tell friends to keep learning the **basics** anyway.
think: I'm a bit **disappointed**, because I find this stuff exciting.
I'd also feel relieved for my **parents'** jobs.
do: Keep using the assistant to learn **faster** and run the study group.
Apply for a summer job at a **small** software company.
Keep **tutoring** school kids in maths online.
feel: Calm but a little **flat**, like a festival with the headline act cancelled.
S0.quote: I'd tell my friend to stay, because a degree still teaches you how to think, and that doesn't expire.
fieldNote: Adaptive and curious; her mild **disappointment** shows she wants AI to matter for good reasons.
Treats the assistant as a coach, not a shortcut.
Money and skills leave nothing weighing on her in a quiet world.

steps.text: Apply for a summer job at a small software company
Keep tutoring two school kids in maths online
Use the AI assistant to quiz herself before every tutorial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the real thing and we should take it seriously, in a good way and a bad way. I'd tell my friends to learn to work with the tools now, and I'd tell my mum's department to teach students how to question AI output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay about myself and worried about a lot of other people. I use these tools daily, so I'm already used to working with them. But a good chunk of entry-level coding and testing jobs would shrink, and my classmates who skip the tools are the ones I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get serious about building things, not just coursework. I'd make two or three small projects that solve real problems, put them online, and join an open-source team. I'd keep tutoring, learn some data and statistics on the side, and use the summer to get a placement where I'm directly working with these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and a bit dizzy, like the first day on a fast ride. I know I'll be okay, and I don't love that I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean you don't love that you know you'll be okay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels unfair. I have parents with money, top grades and a taste for new tools, so I'm the kind of person who lands well. Plenty of people with the same ability but no backup wouldn't. That sits uncomfortably with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your university to do in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop pretending the exams are the same as before. Teach people how to work with the tools, and check understanding in person. I'd also want them to give extra help to students who learned slower, so the gap doesn't widen.

say: I'd say the change is **real** and we should take it seriously.
I'd urge friends to learn the **tools** now and universities to teach questioning AI output.
think: I feel okay about myself and **worried** about others who skip the tools.
I know many entry-level **testing** jobs would shrink.
do: Build two or three **projects** that solve real problems and put them online.
Join an **open-source** team and learn statistics on the side.
Aim the summer at a **placement** working with these tools.
feel: **Exciting** and a bit dizzy, like the first day on a fast ride.
S1.quote: I have parents with money, top grades and a taste for new tools, so I'm the kind of person who lands well.
fieldNote: Calm because of her own position, and **uncomfortable** about it; she names the unfairness.
Most worried about classmates who avoid the tools, not about herself.
Concrete about what a university should change: in-person checks and extra help.

steps.text: Build three small projects that solve real problems and publish them
Join an open-source team and make regular contributions
Get a summer placement working directly with AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need an emergency plan, with public money on income support and retraining, and that the companies building this should have to share what they know. I'd say it online, and I'd write to my mum's union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be really worried, but also fascinated. By 2028 I'd be in second year and everything I'm learning would be done by software. I'd think the most useful thing I could do is work on how this gets made safe and fair, not just how it gets used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my degree, switch toward AI safety and policy courses, and try to get into any research group working on it. I'd also keep tutoring but talk to my parents about being ready to support relatives. And I'd put a few thousand into something boring and safe, because the future is too unclear to gamble with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels huge, like standing on a shore watching the water pull back before a wave. I can't tell whether it's thrilling or terrifying, probably both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you tell if it's thrilling or terrifying, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I picture my own life, it's thrilling, because I'd get to work on the biggest thing happening. When I picture my cousin Hanna, who's a bookkeeper, and my dad's office, it's terrifying. Two years isn't enough for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People like Hanna, mid-career, with a mortgage and a skill that's easy to automate. They'd have the least slack. I'd try to help her by showing her the tools, but I'd know that isn't enough on its own.

say: I'd call for an **emergency plan** with income support and retraining.
I'd say the companies building it must **share** what they know.
think: I'd be really **worried** and also fascinated.
The best thing I could do is work on making it **safe** and fair.
do: Switch toward AI **safety** and policy courses and join a research group.
Keep tutoring and be ready to **support** relatives.
Put a few thousand into something **boring** and safe.
feel: Like watching the water pull back before a **wave**, thrilling and terrifying.
S2.quote: When I picture my cousin Hanna, who's a bookkeeper, and my dad's office, it's terrifying. Two years isn't enough for them.
fieldNote: Her own prospects feel **thrilling**; the fear comes from relatives with mortgages and routine jobs.
Turns toward AI safety and policy, a goal beyond personal career security.
Mood is anxious because her household's and relatives' incomes are exposed, not her own.

steps.text: Switch to AI safety and policy modules next term
Ask research groups about summer work on AI safety
Put a few thousand into a safe savings account
Write to a union branch about emergency retraining pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, so use it. We need rules on how AI is deployed, public funds for retraining, and universities that update courses every year. I'd say this to my course representative and write about it in the student paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel energised. I'd graduate in three years, right inside the window, and I'd be good with the tools by then. The robots come around 2034, so my own area stays safer than most for a while, but the thinking AI will have arrived by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with a strong portfolio, apply to a research master's on AI policy, and work a couple of summers in industry to see what's real. I'd keep tutoring and teach adults who want to learn the tools. Maybe I'd set up a free evening class in the library.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels busy, in a good way. I'd have something to do with the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be mostly reacting and consoling people. With five I could build something, like that library class, or a small tool that helps people retrain. Time turns fear into projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the hardest part for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing I might be wrong about how fast it goes. I'd have made big choices on a forecast, and if the date moves, I'd have to be fine with that. I'd tell myself the skills carry over anyway.

say: I'd say five years is a **window**, so use it with rules and retraining funds.
I'd write in the student paper that courses must **update** yearly.
think: I'd feel **energised**, graduating in three years inside the window.
My own area stays a little **safer** until the robots come around 2034.
do: Finish with a strong **portfolio** and apply to a research master's on AI policy.
Teach adults the tools in a free **evening** class at the library.
Work two **summers** in industry to see what's real.
feel: **Busy** in a good way, with something to do about the worry.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be mostly reacting and consoling people. With five I could build something
fieldNote: Extra time turns her fear into **projects**; she names the library class as one.
Admits she might be wrong about the date and says skills would carry over.
Uneasy rather than anxious: her own path looks open and the strain is in those around her.

steps.text: Apply for a research master's on AI policy
Set up a free evening class on AI tools at the library
Work two summers in industry to see real jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us do this properly: slow retraining that doesn't wreck anyone's life, and schools that teach thinking, not just facts. I'd say people should stay calm but not complacent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. I'd finish a degree, maybe a master's, and probably spend a few years inside the field while it changes. I might even be someone who helps decide the rules. I'd still carry a small worry for the people with less cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and aim high: a research master's, then a job at an organisation that works on AI standards or safety. I'd keep tutoring and keep using the tools every day. I'd also save steadily, and start giving a small amount to a retraining charity once I earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels hopeful, a bit like being at the start of something. I'd still check myself so I'm not just enjoying my own luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stay honest with yourself about your own luck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep spending time with people who aren't like me, like the families I tutor. I'd listen to what they say about work and not just explain. Giving opinions is easy from a nice flat with parents' money behind you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any plan if the date moved closer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd move quicker on the safety side and talk to my family about money earlier. But I'd not drop the degree. Even in the fast scenarios, knowing how things work is what lets you steer.

say: I'd say ten years lets us **retrain** people without wrecking lives.
I'd say stay calm but not **complacent**.
think: I'd feel **good** and maybe help decide the rules.
I'd still carry a small worry for people with less **cushion**.
do: Aim for a research **master's**, then work on AI standards or safety.
Keep **tutoring** and using the tools every day.
Save steadily and **give** to a retraining charity once earning.
feel: **Hopeful**, like the start of something, while checking my own luck.
S4.quote: Giving opinions is easy from a nice flat with parents' money behind you.
fieldNote: A decade makes her **hopeful** but self-aware; she tutors families unlike her own to keep perspective.
Would bring forward plans if the date moved, without abandoning the degree.
Calm fits her money, skills and optimism, and she says so.

steps.text: Aim for a research master's and then a standards or safety job
Keep tutoring families and listen to their views on work
Give a small monthly amount to a retraining charity once earning

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, mostly for other people. I'd be fine, but my cousin Hanna and the families I tutor wouldn't have time. What would help is paid retraining and a clear public plan before any of it starts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people shouldn't mistake a confident student for a safe world. I'm adaptable because I've been given room to be. I'd like that room spread around.

headlineQuote: I'm adaptable because I've been given room to be. I'd like that room spread around.
portrait: Carla is an 18-year-old **computer science** student who uses an AI assistant every day and has no money worries.
She is curious and optimistic about the tools, and tutors school kids and runs a study group.
She leans left, wants public retraining and rules, and is uncomfortable about how much her **family money** helps.
Her own path feels open in most pictures; her fear is for relatives like her cousin Hanna.
She turns anxious only in the **two-year** picture and treats longer warnings as time to build things.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, mostly for others who would have no time to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** and a clear public plan before it starts.
